utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. May I ask the registrar to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I have appearances for the Defence -- sorry, Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, counsel. For the Prosecution, David Re and Ekkehard Withopf with Kimberly Fleming as the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am Edina Residovic with Stephane Bourgon for Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. For Mr. Kubura, Mr. Rodney Dixon, Mr. Ibrisimovic. And Mr. Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We have received an application from the Office of the Prosecutor for protection measures. We, therefore, order a closed session for the complete protection of the witness. May I ask the registrar to take the necessary steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are again in public session. And the voice of the witness should now be distorted, as well as his image. Witness, we shall address you with the pseudonym BA, because of the protective measures granted you. Will you now please read the solemn declaration. The usher is giving you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Try again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems there is a problem with the microphone. May I ask the witness, can you hear the interpretation? He does. It seems to be a technical problem with the microphone. Madam Registrar, could we change the microphone or do something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to wait for a technical assistant who will check the microphone. All right. Witness BA, will you please read again the text of the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You can sit down. So the Prosecution may begin their examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness BA, I'm going to refer to you throughout your examination-in-chief as Witness BA, and we will move into private session for some parts of your evidence, those parts which may identify you. Witness BA, you were a member of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH in 1992, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Counsel, you just told us that we will have to go into private session occasionally. You will indicate, I hope, the moments when we have to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I certainly will, Your Honour. And I will very shortly do so, at the beginning of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness WB, you were a member of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH in 1992/1993, 1993 and 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] You are objecting and you claim that this is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me remind you only that the Prosecution has just asked him whether he had been a member of the 7th Brigade. I really don't think that it is a leading question. He was at the time either a civilian or as a soldier, and he is being asked whether he was a soldier and whether he was a member of the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness BA, I'm now going to ask you - don't answer the question Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. yet - about the circumstances of your joining the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But could we move into private session for that part of his testimony, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Registrar, let us now go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness BA, can you see a photograph on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you identify that as a photograph of the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this was a leading question, quite obviously. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution should have phrased the question by asking the witness whether he recognised the photograph and by asking the witness to tell us what he could tell on the basis of the photograph. Let's continue, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The photograph has a -- a number, 01247564, with the Prosecution Exhibit number P1306.84. It's in Sanction. Can the photograph be marked for identification for the moment in Sanction and we will provide the Trial Chamber with copies of it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, the Defence doesn't have any objections to tendering this photograph into evidence? No objections? Could you give me a definitive number for this photograph then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I note the registrar said marked for identification. I understood Your Honours to be accepting the tender of that photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P7, not marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness BA, whereabouts were you based or was your unit based in the Music School -- or as depicted on the photograph P7 on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: It was based in the premises of this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness BA, you can see on the photograph which is in front of you, on the right-hand side it has three levels, four windows on the bottom floor, four windows on the middle floor, and some smaller ones on the top floor. All I want to know is physically where in the building was your unit based until January 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I can't remember quite clearly whether it was based on the first floor or the attic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to tell us how the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was using that building when you were based there, up until January 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: It was used by the soldiers as a place where they would spend time while they were in the unit. That was the main purpose for which it was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness BA, were you familiar with the various floors in the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the basement of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade using the basement for up until January 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: It was used as a warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the brigade storing in the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Mainly the surplus of weapons and foodstuff for the needs of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you a photograph which again will come up on the screen in front of you. What can you tell me about the photograph which bears the description 0124-7575, Prosecution number P1306.29?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: The basement of the Music School, which is where we had accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that photograph likewise be tendered into evidence through Sanction, and the Prosecution will provide the Trial Chamber with copies later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There are no objections from the Defence. Could we have a number for the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the number will be P8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Later in your evidence, Witness BA, I will be asking you about the attack on the village of Dusina. Where was your unit based at the time of the attack on Dusina? Was it still based in the Music School or was it based somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: It was based in the Music School.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did your unit go -- I'm sorry. Until when was your unit based in the Music School?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but when we returned from Dusina we returned to Bilmiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you returned to Bilmiste. What is -- what is and where is Bilmiste, Witness BA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Bilmiste was an educational centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: By that do you mean school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: There were three schools there before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When your unit moved there, were there any other units already there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Whereabouts is Bilmiste?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it in -- was Zenica -- it in Zenica? Sorry. Is Bilmiste, the school or the educational facility, in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to show you a map, Witness BA. It's a map of the town of Zenica headed "Series M903, sheet Zenica, addition 1 GSGS."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, Your Honours, I'm going to have to do this one the old-fashioned way and have the witness actually mark on a paper copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I want you to mark on the map with a round circle and a "1" is where Bilmiste is. I want you to mark with a "2" where the Zenica Music School is. And I want you to mark with a "3" where the 3rd Corps headquarters was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On our screens we can see a -- a map of the town of Zenica, which contains three circles, which refer to the three questions put by the Prosecution. I want to know whether this is what the witness can see or is the witness marking the location of certain sites according to his own memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, when you marked the map with the numbers "1", 2", "3", did you do this directly on the basis of the big map or did you do it on the small map on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only on this map here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He used -- he marked the map with these numbers without looking at the screen; that's what he has just told us. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to know whether the markings were the same on the map that he was looking at. That's all I am interested in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's necessary to know what he has marked. Could you bring the big map to me, please. The Trial Chamber will check. We have a big map here, and I can see that where it says "cemetery," it's been marked with number "1." At the site where it says "building 398 metres," it's been marked with number "2." And the number "3" is at the top of the map. We have a service in black. So perhaps he should tell us -- Witness, number 1 -- you used number "1" to mark which site? Could you show him the map. So number "1" refers to what exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the locality where the school is, corresponds to the site of the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about number "2"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the site of the music school. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So number 2 refers to the music school. And what about number 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the 3rd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 3 marks the 3rd Corps command. Very well. Did you want to tender this map into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I just have a look at what the witness has marked on it first, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please show it to the Defence. And could you show it to the accused as well. They haven't seen the map on their screens. Please continue. So you want to tender this map into evidence, Mr. Re? Could we have a number for the map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P9.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've told us about the 2nd Battalion, Witness BA. Where was the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade based from January 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: In Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Whereabouts in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: In the Sretno Motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to show you a photograph, which will be on your screen. Can you please look at the photograph on the screen and tell Their Honours whether you can identify it and what it is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes. It's the Sretno Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And whereabouts is it located in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: It's by the motorway, at the entrance to Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where does that motorway go in either direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: It's the Zenica-Sarajevo motorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I tender that one too into evidence through Sanction, to provide the registry and the Trial Chamber with a copy of it later.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Registrar, the number is P10. P10. However, I would like to note, with regard to tendering this into evidence, it's a hotel but sometimes it is referred to as a motel. It's not the same thing, a motel and a hotel; these are quite different things. And I think that in the indictment it says the "Sretno Motel," but we can see quite clearly that it is a hotel and not a motel. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness BA, when you were in the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, did you ever have any -- sorry, did you ever go into the Motel or Hotel Sretno when the 1st Battalion was using it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've told me about the 1st Battalion and the 2nd Battalion. Now, what about the 3rd Battalion? Where was it based?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion was based in bell mist -- Bilmiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was the commander of your battalion in 1993, from the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I can't remember his exact name. I think it was Commander Taran.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to tell Their Honours about the structure of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade from January 1993. There were three Battalions: The 1st, the 2nd, and the 3rd. What other units were there in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: At the time, the brigade was still being formed. Not a single unit had been officially formed. Its formation had not officially been completed. They were still in the process of completion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When do you consider it was fully formed; that is, the three brigades were formed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: At the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to tell the Trial Chamber about the way the soldiers in the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade were paid. What were your wages per month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: There were no pays before the formation -- when the army was being formed. Later, when the corps started issuing salaries, we received about 80 marks, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the other soldiers in the ABiH being paid in this period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: It depended on the manoeuvre capacities of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the difference between your brigade and the other brigades in -- in relation to the manoeuvre capacities of the units and what they were being paid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: For the most part, all manoeuvring sabotage units had higher pay than those that only held the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The wages of your unit were 80 Deutschemarks -- I'm sorry. You said your wages -- the wages of your unit were something like 80 marks a month. What were the wages of the other units, the non-manoeuvring units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: They were paid 40 Deutschemark, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How was the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade equipped? Who supplied it with equipment, arms, supplies, uniforms, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: It was equipped better than other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: In terms of the appearance of our soldiers as compared to members of other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said it was better equipped than the other units. Who was supplying the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade? Where was it getting its armed, equipment, supplies and so on, from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where it received them from.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why do you say it was better equipped than the other units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I'm saying that because it was better equipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the reason for it being better equipped than the other units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the uniform of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms, just as every other member.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence. The noise is still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think we missed the last part of your sentence. The interpreter heard you say "they wore camouflage uniforms, just as every other member." Did you say something else after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: No. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did the uniforms the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade wore compare to that of other units and brigades within the ABiH 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: The logistics always supplied new uniforms, so every new member would get a uniform. In some units, people wore used uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of training did the 3rd -- sorry, the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade give its soldiers? Can I -- I'll withdraw that question. I'll start with another question. The 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was called a Muslim Mountain Brigade. What was the difference between it and other brigades in the ABiH 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We seem to have a microphone problem again. Did you hear the question that was asked? Would the usher be so kind as to check the microphone. Very well. The Prosecution may continue. The witness now hears.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was called a Muslim Mountain Brigade. What was the difference between it and other brigades in the ABiH 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: It was made up only of Muslims, while other units comprised also Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why was this particular brigade composed only of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Because it was called the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the military reason for having a separate brigade composed only of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness is now being asked for his opinion, and I believe that a regular witness should not dispense opinions of the kind that the Prosecution is asking at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Defence counsel believe that this is a question of view, of opinion. So will you please rephrase your question. But the Chamber reserves the right to stop such questions in the future but -- or to allow them, but right now you are being asked to rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness BA, you gave evidence about when and how you joined the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. Were you ever told or did you ever ask anyone who had the knowledge or the authority to tell you why, if indeed -- I'm sorry, ask if there was a military reason for there being a brigade composed entirely of Muslims? And if so, what the answer was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only is an opinion being asked now. The Prosecutor wants the witness to give us hearsay, which is not allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This objection is sustained. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mrs. Residovic just said hearsay isn't allowed. If I could direct Your Honours to Rule -- just give me one moment -- Rule 89. I can't pin at this particular -- at this moment -- I'm sorry, I can't direct Your Honours to any jurisprudence or decisions of the Appeals or Trial Chambers at the moment as I stand here, but hearsay is certainly allowed in this Tribunal. The question is the probative value and the weight that the Trial Chamber gives it when assessing the evidence. So what my learned friend has put to Your Honours is simply incorrect, about hearsay not being allowed. I can certainly locate the cases, but I just can't do it as I stand here, and provide them to Your Honours later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber will resolve this by asking a question of the witness, because the Trial Chamber has the right to do so at any moment. So, Witness BA, could you please tell us, in your view were there any other brigades that were Muslim brigades or Muslim units within your corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the witness tells us he didn't know if there were any other such units similar to that 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. To his knowledge -- or rather, he has no knowledge of the structure within his corps. Another question to the witness: Apart from your comrades who fought with you in that Muslim brigade, you have no knowledge of other units; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His answer is, therefore that, he has no knowledge whatsoever about the structure of the corps, apart from the brigade where he fought.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness BA, I want you to tell the Trial Chamber about the badges worn by the soldiers in the various 3rd Corps units and, of course, your own brigade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: For the most part, all members wore the emblems of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you describe the emblem of the 3rd Corps to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: On a patch of cloth initials of the 3rd Corps were inscribed, together with the initials of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the badge of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: We had a badge of the 3rd Corps, and in addition to that there was lettering "7th Muslim."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just said that your unit had both a 7th Muslim lettering and the 3rd Corps initials -- or emblem, I'm sorry. Did each brigade or unit have its own badge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Some units had their own emblems.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to have a look at Exhibit P4, which will come up on the screen in front of you. Witness BA, can you see 24 representations with numbers on the screen in front of you in Sanction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what number 12 is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: That's the army emblem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did the members of your brigade wear that emblem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Some did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say "some," can you give the Trial Chamber a rough percentage of those who did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you yourself wear number 12 on your uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you wear any other badges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are any of those two depicted on Exhibit 4 -- sorry, P4, in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Both of them can be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What numbers are those, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: 9 and 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What precisely is number 9?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: That's the badge -- sorry, the patch of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did all soldiers in the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade wear that badge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Not all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did those who didn't wear that badge wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Some simply didn't wear patches, because there weren't enough of them to go round.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please have a look at badge number 7. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what badge number 7 is and whether it relates to badge number 12.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: What they have in common is the coat of arms and the lilies, and the rest ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know what badge number 7 is, Witness BA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that question precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention to badge number 1. What is badge number 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: That is the patch of the Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the Muslim armed forces, Witness BA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I could not answer this precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You say you can't answer it precisely, but you're able to tell us that it is the badge of the Muslim armed forces. How do you know that it is the badge of the Muslim amend forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: It is written around the lower edge, "Muslim armed forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you know of someone called Mahmut Efendija Karalic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was he in 1992? What position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly his position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you know of him at that time, 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I knew that he was a hodza and that he used to be a professor at the Sarajevo University.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the entirety of this answer. There may be something missing. The noise is still terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness BA, there may have been a slight difficulty of interpretation of your last answer. I don't know. Did you say "I knew that he was a hodza and that he used to be a professor at the Sarajevo University," or did you add something to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I said he was a hodza and a professor in the Sarajevo Muslim school, Medresa.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber -- sorry. Can you please give the Trial Chamber an explanation of what a hodza is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Hodza is a spiritual leader of a community.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you know of a person called Asim Suvalic in about 1992 to 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Only the name is familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How is the name familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence may speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot exactly call these questions formally leading, but the Prosecutor always mentions a name that had not been previously referred to by the witness. He first gives a name and then only asks if the witness knows anything about the person. So I think that, essentially, these are leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber is of the view that the question is indeed leading because you are asking questions about the person named Suvalic in this case. I think it would be better to rephrase the question; to ask, for instance, what "hodza" means and whether he knew anyone who held that position. That is one of the ways in which this question could have been formulated. Of course, the Defence's job is to protect the interests of the accused and to take care that no leading questions are asked of witnesses. This is a question of form. Would you be so kind as to rephrase the question as to avoid leading the witness. Continue, please, and we shall take care that no more leading questions are asked. It is a fact that if the witness is led to a name that seems to come out of the blue, it may be a problem. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please, Your Honours, could I just have a moment. I need to check something on LiveNote, the transcript, before I go on. The screen in front of me, as you know, Your Honours, is only about a page long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you consulted the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. I worked out the question I asked before. Your Honours will appreciate sometimes you forget the question you asked before an interruption and you've got to go back and look at it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness BA, do you know who the leaders of the MOS were in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The words you just used were "I don't know exactly." What do you mean by "I don't know exactly"? Can you clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "clarifying."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question was: "Do you know who the leaders were in 1992 and 1993?", and your answer was "I don't know exactly." Do you know any other way other than exactly? Do you have some partial knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you please go back to Exhibit P4, which -- which is the badges in front of you. Can you please look at number 15. What can you tell the Trial Chamber about badge number 15?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what it says? It has some Arabic writing on it. Can you read that to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I cannot read Arabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please look at number 19. Have you seen badges similar to that before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: At the bazaar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which bazaar and where and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: One of -- in fact, some of these emblems can be obtained in several places by anyone: civilians, soldiers, anybody. They were used as some sort of advertisement item.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did soldiers of your brigade or any of the other brigades in the 3rd Corps wear a badge similar to number 19 during 1992, 1993, and 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Every soldier was able to get hold of any patch and put it on his sleeve. You could even buy an emblem of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just to direct you to number 19. Do you remember seeing soldiers in either your brigade or other brigades wearing badges similar to that shown in number 19?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just tell the Trial Chamber what the lettering at the bottom says, not the Arabic, the letter that goes round -- the lettering that goes round the bottom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: "Muslim forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I note it's 4.15, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For technical reasons, we shall take a break. We will resume in 20 minutes. It is now 4.15. We will reconvene at 4.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] Very well. I think that in order to organise our work, we can continue until quarter to 6.00, then we'll have a 20-minute break and carry on until 7.00. So we have an hour -- an hour and ten minutes of examination or cross-examination perhaps too. That depends on the amount of time that will remain to us. The Prosecution may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To finish be the badges, Witness BA, can you please look at numbers 17 and 24. Firstly, can you tell the Trial Chamber anything about number 17?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I've never seen badge number 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And number 24?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: It's not correctly written, but I haven't seen this one either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "it's not correctly written"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Well, quite simply it's not correctly written.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You told us before the break about what a hodza was. Did your unit of the 7th Mountain Brigade have a hodza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was your hodza and what was his role?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: There were several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is there a difference between a hodza and an emir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain to the Trial Chamber what the difference is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: A hodza would take care of religious rites with the soldiers, for the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the emir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: The emir was responsible for issues which were outside of that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Like ...?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly, but I know that all the hodzas in the brigade were accountable to the emir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And who was the emir of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Mahmut Efendija Karalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did the soldiers of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade receive religious instruction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Every member had access to the Koran [realtime transcript read in error "corps"] and could learn something about the religion in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Apart from access to the Koran, did the soldiers in the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade receive religious instruction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sure. I asked you whether soldiers of your brigade received religious instruction, and you told me that every member had access to the Koran and could learn something about religion in this way. What I'm asking you is did the soldiers actually receive any religious instruction as part of being a member of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness has already answered this question, but according to the transcript he didn't only mention the Koran. He said that all the soldiers were able to receive various forms of religious instruction. Now, I don't understand the Prosecution's question, because the witness did not just mention the Koran.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Prosecution may continue. The witness mentioned access to religious instruction but not just access to the Koran. It wasn't just based on the Koran. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question and answer at 36, line 16.40 is: Did the soldiers receive any religious instruction? The answer was: "Every member had access to the" -- it says "corps" but it was "Koran" -- "and could learn something about the religion in this way." That's the question and answer I have in the transcript. I was asking the witness to elaborate on that. Apart from access to the Koran, was there any formal religious instruction or was it part of your duties as -- or part of the fact that you were a member of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade? That part wasn't quite answered. I'm just reading what the transcript actually says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will resolve this issue by asking the witness. As far as your religious instruction was concerned, was there a religious person who would provide you with such instruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every member of the 7th Muslim Brigade could obtain information that he was interested in, given that 95 per cent -- that members of the brigade were 100 per cent Muslim, so they already had access to this instruction. Anyone who was interested could ask for access to such literature in order to study it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this literature, what was it exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly religious literature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not just the Koran then? There were other religious books?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has just told us that there were various kinds of religious books. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness BA, upon joining the Muslim -- 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, what documents did the members, the new members, sign?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: They signed a document that was the brigade's code.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the brigade's code?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: The brigade's code was based on human and eastern rights, on the rights of Muslims and non-Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many parts did the code have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I think it had six or seven parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the parts in relation -- or in respect of Muslim rites -- that's r-i-t-e-s.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: All members of the 7th Muslim Brigade had to practice religious rites and they had to respect their religion and the Muslims' tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were those aspects of Muslim tradition that they had to respect specified in this code?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: It mostly meant that the Islam tradition had to be respected. Each member of the 7th Muslim Brigade was not to consume alcohol. So it concerned matters that were related to the Islam religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said the brigade's code was based on human and eastern rights, also on the rights of non-Muslims. What were the human and non-Muslim rights contained in that code?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Well, one of the items in the code concerned human rights and the Geneva Conventions, the rights that were applicable in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were those, to the best of your recollection, that were specified in this code?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: At was necessary to respect the rules of war, POWs' rights had to be respected. They weren't to be killed. It related to the Geneva Conventions, on the whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Apart from those things specified in the code, were you or other soldiers, to your knowledge, given instruction on the laws of war or the Geneva Conventions, the rights of POWs, et cetera, while you were a member of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to tell the Trial Chamber how and when that occurred and how many times.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: As soon as we signed this code, we were informed of these rules, of the duties of members of the 7th Muslim Brigade and of the rights of other people in certain other situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you were informed. I just want you to tell the Trial Chamber briefly how. Like, where it was and who did the -- who did the informing, what sort of information you were given, and how long this went for.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Apart from the initial instruction, when you -- when members joined, were members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade given any further instruction on the Geneva Conventions, rights of POWs, laws of war, et cetera, at any other time after joining?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you recall any -- receiving any other instruction on the laws of war, all those things I just referred to? And if so, when and where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Our attention was drawn to the duties of members of the 7th Muslim Brigade on several occasions, on our duties in a time of war. But I just can't remember when this was done exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll take you back to the other part that you told us about, of the code which related to the Islamic -- or the Muslim portion, that is, not to drink alcohol and to respect the Islamic traditions. Were you aware of any situations when soldiers breached the Islamic component of the code?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did that involve? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: They took disciplinary measures against such soldiers, in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I'll come to that in a moment. Maybe my question was ambiguous. What did the soldiers do? What was -- what breach did the soldiers commit of the Islamic component of the code?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: That mostly had to do with drinking alcohol and committing other minor offences outside the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the disciplinary measures taken against soldiers who were drinking alcohol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: It depended on what that involved. Some people were problematic in addition to the fact that they drank alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to tell the Trial Chamber of any specific incidents you know of of people who were drinking alcohol being disciplined by the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, what the soldiers did, and what the discipline -- what the disciplining involved.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Some were sent out of the unit. They were placed at the disposal of the corps. Some people were placed in detention, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said some were placed in detention. Where were they placed in detention and for how long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: For one, two, or three days, or for a week. It depended.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And where was the detention centre where they were placed? Which one was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: It was in the gymnasium, Bilmiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who placed them there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You also said apart from soldiers who had been -- soldiers being disciplined for drinking alcohol, some soldiers were disciplined for committing crimes outside. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber of specific instances you know of soldiers within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade being disciplined for committing crimes outside.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just told us a moment ago about soldiers being disciplined, detained for drinking alcohol. Before that, you referred to soldiers being disciplined for committing crimes outside. I think you meant outside of the unit. What I want you to do is to tell the Trial Chamber of any specific instances you know of of soldiers who committed crimes outside of the unit and how they were disciplined and what the crimes were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: In the case of theft, for example. There were cases of theft, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the discipline -- I'm sorry, I withdraw that. How were soldiers who stole outside the unit disciplined?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: They would be placed in detention or discharged from the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you aware of soldiers being placed in detention in other centres apart from the gymnasium in Bilmiste?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And do you know whether the case of theft you were referring to -- referring ago -- referring to a minute ago - I'm sorry - was dealt with as a disciplinary -- were dealt with as disciplinary or criminal matters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We've just been speaking about the code which every soldier in the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade had to sign. Were the soldiers given a copy of the code?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I can't remember whether the soldiers were provided with a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to show you another document, which should be on the screen in front of you now. If you look to the left side of the screen, you'll see a document, the English translation is "Instructions to the Muslim Fighter," Zenica 1993. The author is Hafiz Halil Mehtic and Professor Hasan Makic. I want you to tell the Trial Chamber what the document on the left side of the screen is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: This document contained instructions that concerned the religion of soldiers who perhaps were not familiar with certain religious matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who received this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Each and every soldier had access to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you receive a copy of this document yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I consulted some of the literature that was available, but I don't remember whether I had a look at this copy. I don't remember whether I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said each and every soldier had access to this document. How did they have access to it? Where was the document kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: When you read the title "Instructions to the Muslim Fighter," the impression that -- well, these instructions, it was a book that stated how a Muslim soldier could perform the rites. These weren't instructions for soldiers, as soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did the soldiers have access to the book? What do you mean by "they had access to it"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: You would just report to your hodza in the unit and say that you needed some of the literature. The hodza would make an effort to provide you with the literature you required.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that be tendered into evidence now in B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't recall hearing that the witness recognised this document, because we aren't familiar with the contents. It would be necessary to ask the witness whether he is aware of the contents of these instructions. He mentioned instructions that had to do with religious rites, so I'm not sure that the witness has recognised this document, which the Prosecution is now presenting as a piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will ask the witness a question. Witness, the document that you have before you, were you provided with a copy when you became a member of the 7th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember exactly whether I had this document and whether it was available to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see this document at the site or did comrades of yours have copies of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that this is the first time you are seeing it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The title of this little booklet does not matter. What matters is the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As to the contents then. Have you familiarised yourself with them? Have you read the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you cannot tell us anything about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am turning, therefore, to the Prosecution. The witness is telling us that he cannot say anything about this book and even less about the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just consult the transcript a few pages back, when I first asked him? The witness, Your Honour, has given evidence of familiarity with the title of the book and its meaning and the fact that it was available to soldiers in the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade upon request from a hodza. The witness's evidence is that he himself can't remember - I think is what he said - he said he doesn't know whether he's read the book himself. The Prosecution isn't tendering the book on the basis that this witness himself read the book but that this was a book which -- a booklet, which this witness can identify, was available upon request from the hodza within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade to the soldiers there. Whether or not this witness is aware of the contents is immaterial. It's the fact that this particular book, and its contents, of course, were available to the soldiers there. The Prosecution moves to admit it at this point and it will obviously become far more relevant later in the trial when we possibly can produce other evidence linking to it. So at this stage it's only -- I'm only moving for its admission on the basis this witness can identify the fact that the book -- the title of the book and that it was available in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm turning to the witness. The Prosecutor has just indicated that this document apparently, at the moment when you were in the 7th Brigade, is a document of whose existence you knew and you could have acquainted yourself with the contents if you had wished to. I'm asking you: Even if you didn't hold it in your hands, did you know that this document existed? I am very careful in phrasing this question. Did you know of the existence of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The witness asserts that he doesn't know. In view of this state of affairs, I think we will mark this document for identification and see later what we can do with it, since the Prosecution claims that members of the 7th Muslim Brigade had this document and the witness is not confirming this claim. We will give this document a number for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me also draw the attention of those present to another difficulty. When the Prosecution tenders a document, all the parties need to be supplied with a copy, which makes a total of seven copies. The registrar is telling me they don't have a copy; the Trial Chamber doesn't have one either; and I don't think the Defence has the document either. When you are submitting a document, be so kind as to provide seven copies. In view of your resources, I don't believe that that would be a problem. At the moment, we cannot include this document even provisionally, unless you have additional copies to provide right now. So we will give a provisional number to this document for the time being and we hope to get a copy from you tomorrow. Could the registrar please give me a provisional number for this document, because right now it doesn't exist for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exhibit number will be P11 for the B/C/S version and P11E for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this stage makes one observation in respect of this part of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That being the effect of the Trial Chamber's ruling, I think last Wednesday. In relation to refreshing memory from a witness's statement means, I take it, we can't show the witness's statement to the witness in the witness box, to ask him to refresh his memory where he said "I don't know" at this point. I'm flagging this so that Your Honours are aware that if the Prosecution files another document -- makes another filing in respect of Your Honours' motion -- sorry, Your Honours' ruling last week, Your Honours are alerted to this passage, this potential exhibit in this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Before I give the floor to Counsel Bourgon, I must remind everyone of the following: The Trial Chamber does not have the statement of this witness, so we don't know what this witness stated before. As regards this particular document, the witness says he cannot say anything at all. The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my learned friend wishes to make comments regarding some previous statements, in the light of the Trial Chamber's last week's decision, then the witness should be ushered out of the courtroom first so we can have a free discussion of the issue. I don't think this issue needs to be raised now in the presence of the witness because that would be tantamount to giving the witness his own statement to remind him of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence rightfully reminds us that if you wish to refresh the witness's memory, it cannot be done under a decision that the Trial Chamber had not been made aware of; and second, if a previous statement is to be discussed, it can only be done so in the absence of the witness. Otherwise, he might be unduly warned of the issues at hand. It would be tantamount to telling the witness "in paragraph such and such you said this and that and today you are saying something quite different". It is quite possible that certain things elude someone's memory momentarily, and that's why I said it would be a good idea to mark this document provisionally. For the time being, we have no elements in front of us that would allow us to judge that the witness really knows about it. You can ask, however, if the witness knows anything about the content from his comrades. For instance, the Trial Chamber knows nothing of this issue, apart from what we heard today in the courtroom. You may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My comment was only directed to -- that the Prosecution intends to file a document in response to Your Honours' ruling. I'm just alerting Your Honours to it may impact upon this witness's -- in passing. That's all. I'm not debating the issue with the Defence or the Trial Chamber, and especially not in the witness's presence. And I'm certainly not asking Your Honours to reconsider at the moment. I'm just flagging that there may be some impact. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But it cannot be done in the presence of the witness. I would like to deal with this situation in this way: I'll ask the witness directly. Witness BA, we have just discussed the document, which as you told us you never had and never read. Maybe you discussed it with your comrades, friends.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you never talked about this document with any of your comrades; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you never saw this document in your base in which you were stationed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is the first time that you are seeing this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. He is telling us that he hasn't seen this document before and he hasn't talked about it with his comrades and he doesn't know what's in it. It may seem like a contradiction as compared with his statement, but that's what it is. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If Your Honours would just excuse me for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When His Honour the Presiding Judge a moment ago asked you, Witness BA, whether you had seen this document before, did you understand His Honour to be referring to in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I saw it on that paper that you showed me, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. And was that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the Prosecution interviewed you in 2002, and you provided a statement to the Prosecution. Do you remember seeing that book when the Prosecution interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember my providing you with a copy of this statement yesterday to take back to your hotel with you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was sure the Defence was going to be on their feet. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My learned friend is now doing precisely what the Trial Chamber prohibited by their last week's decision; namely, the Prosecutor is making the witness aware of a part of his earlier statement by quoting it. He says, "I showed you this and you said that," and he's trying to get the answers he needs in a different way. This all looks like cross-examination to me; although, it should not be cross-examination. If my learned friend wishes to ask questions regarding the witness's statement and what the witness had done, seen, or heard, it can be done in the absence of the witness. But the Prosecutor should by no means be allowed to examine the witness in this way and jog his memory here in the way that was forbidden by the Trial Chamber's decision. There certainly are other ways to achieve the same goal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. With regard to this important issue, the Trial Chamber wishes to underline the following: In these proceedings, the Office of the Prosecutor questioned this witness in the course of investigation and the witness provided a witness statement, a written statement. Several months later the witness comes here to the courtroom to give evidence viva voce. In the course of a proofing session, before the witness appears in the courtroom, the Prosecution talks to him again and refreshes his memory. During the proceedings, however, the witness gives a solemn declaration, a declaration we need to believe; otherwise, we could have doubts about false testimony. During viva voce testimony the witness says that he had never seen that document in his country while he was a soldier. He only said that he saw the document yesterday during a proofing session. It is almost certain, therefore, that sometime ago, several years ago, the witness said he had seen the document but in the meantime he changed his mind and he is now stating he doesn't remember, he is not sure; and here before the Judges he says he never saw the document until yesterday. That's all we can note as regards this document. He may very well have told you yesterday, in response to your question, that he did see it before, but what matters is what he says here before the Judges under oath and under oath today, what he says is, "I haven't seen this document before." And from what we understood, he is not even aware of its contents. I believe that's how the land lies. I understand that the tasks faced by the Prosecution are complex and they are facing a difficult situation because the witness seems to be saying something different to what he said before, but what matters is what he says before the Judges. Of course, the Trial Chamber will hear other witnesses and hear other evidence on the same issue, but this witness right now is saying that he knows nothing of it. Please continue. Our time is precious, and I believe there must be more important issues that you can raise with this witness. We have 15 minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not attempting to cross-examine the witness. I think Mr. Bourgon misunderstood what I was doing. I was simply asking the witness whether I gave him a copy of the statement last night, in relation to a -- a filing the Prosecution intends to file in the very near future in of Your Honours's ruling. That is as far as I wish to take it, just to establish the foundation for a submission I wish to make. That's as far as I wish to take it, Your Honours. May I receive an answer as to whether I gave him a copy to refresh, in line of Your Honours's decision -- not to refresh, to take home with him. That was the extent of that, and as far as I want to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Go ahead and ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness BA, last night did I give you a copy of your statement to take back to your hotel with you to read?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Earlier in your evidence, Witness BA, you told us about the badges and camouflage uniform that your unit wore. What other things did your -- what other items of apparel, if any, did your unit wear, apart from a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: In certain situations, depending on the weather and some other factors, we would wear some different uniforms, if that's what you were driving at.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did your wear on your head when you went into battle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes, we did; although, it was not compulsory.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The answer is not quite clear. What did you wear on your heads when you went into battle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: We wore headbands, just as an identification thing, headbands that helped us distinguish amongst each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What colour were the headbands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Green or black.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was anything written on the headbands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Something in Arabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know what it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Lajlahelala.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what's that in Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I'm not a really good translator from Arabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Doing your best...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I would not like to even try.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said it was to distinguish -- help to distinguish amongst each other. Who was being distinguished? From whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear what you mean. Distinguished for whom, from whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said "we wore headbands as identification things, headbands that helped us distinguish amongst each other." I want you to elaborate on that, to explain to the Trial Chamber who was being distinguished. Why were you wearing the headbands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: In order to ask that question, you need to know a few things about this war. If bullets are whizzing around your head, you see things differently than you would see them if you just saw that on television, looking from your home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you mean you were trying to distinguish your side from the other side or your side from -- or your unit from other units or soldiers from civilians? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: For the most part, if we had a head-on clash with the enemy and we worked in cooperation with other units from the same side, then we needed to distinguish among various units on our side. Sometimes these headbands were yellow or red or green. It all depended on the particular operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you wore different uniforms, depending upon weather conditions. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what different uniforms you wore.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Not all members of the 7th Muslim Brigade wore uniforms of different colours. The colour of the uniforms depended on the weather. If there was snow on the ground, we wore white uniforms. By night-time, sabotage units and reconnaissance units would wear black uniforms. It all depend on the configuration of terrain, the weather, and other conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about flags? Did your unit or the brigade have flags?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Every brigade has its own flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade's flag? Can you do your best to describe it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I'm afraid of making a mistake. As far as I can remember, it was black. It had a golden wreath around the edges, and it had the inscription "The 7th Muslim Brigade," and "Lajlahelala," if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did it have any similarity to the badge you pointed out to us before? Which should be coming up on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm showing the witness P4 again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: They didn't really have any similarities with these badges here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where was the flag of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade flown?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: In front of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've mentioned barracks at Bilmiste, the Zenica Music School and Sretno, in Kakanj. Was it flown outside each of those barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I can't remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the ABiH? Did it have a flag as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: We always had a flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking about the ABiH. Did the ABiH have a flag?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: It had the coat of arms of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the flag of the BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that flag flown outside the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it flown at the same time as the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade flag?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: The army flag was always flown, and the 7th Muslim Brigade flag was only used on special occasions, on festive occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of things did members of your unit or brigade say when they went into battle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: There was an Islam greeting that would be used. That's how all of the operations commenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the Islam greeting that was used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: Tekbir Allah-U-Ekber.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is there another way of saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just repeat your answer, please. The question was: Is there another way of saying Tekbir Allah-U-Ekber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: There's no other way of saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said an Islam greeting -- you said those words would be used at the commencement of operations. How did members of your unit use it? What did you say -- sorry, how did you say it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: That was the greeting. One would say Tekbir, and the others would reply, " Allah-U-Ekber."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you're giving this evidence, are you referring to a personal greeting to another member of the brigade? Did you not hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I hear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. When giving this evidence, are you referring to a personal greeting to another member of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: That was a greeting used within the brigade as well. It was a way of supporting the morale of the men. It was also used in the field, once operations had started.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How was it used in the field once operation were started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your unit's particular role in combat operations in Central Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that question precisely. I wouldn't know what to say about its precise role.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When your unit went into battle, what was its position in the battle -- in combat in relation to other units that were also employed in a particular combat operation? Where did your brigade -- or your unit feature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA
utterances.text: If we were billeted in places where there were Muslim inhabitants, we had better support as members of the 7th Muslim Brigade than other units did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's quarter to 6.00. We'll have a break until five past 6.00. But I think that -- How much more time does the Prosecution need?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The way we're moving -- Your Honours are aware from the summary file that there are three specific incidents - that's Vares, Susanj, Ovnak, and Dusina - I haven't got to those yet. I might not finish, unfortunately, today with this witness, the way we're going. I was hoping to, but I don't know whether I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we will have the cross-examination, it's going to be necessary for the witness to return tomorrow. So we will have a break until five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
